call_overview.title: About the call
call_overview.question: What does the call offer, and who can apply?

cards.title: What the call wants
cards.question: What is the principal thing the project must develop, and which problem or need must it address?
cards.answer:
Foundational research on new cryptographic building blocks and protocols for future networks that mix classical and quantum communication, going beyond Quantum Key Distribution.
Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a method that uses quantum physics to share secret keys; the topic asks for new primitives (basic cryptographic building blocks, such as signatures or commitments) and protocols beyond it. Proposals should target some of these areas and end with a roadmap:
- quantum primitives that have a classical equivalent, new quantum primitives impossible classically, and improvements of quantum protocols using classical or post-quantum cryptography (encryption designed to resist quantum computers), for example in run time, energy use or hardware needs
- analysis of how strong and applicable the results are compared with the best classical-only solutions, with rigorous security proofs
- links between quantum information processing and cryptography, such as position verification (proving where a party is located) based on entanglement
- a quantum cryptography roadmap identifying the challenges of building and scaling quantum-network applications
The need comes from the research community: future entanglement-based quantum networks will need a new cryptographic foundation that may require entirely new paradigms.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Civil Security for Society · pp. 171–173 · HORIZON-CL3-2027-02-CS-ECCC-04, Expected outcome and Scope

cards.title: Project impact
cards.question: Which wider system outcomes and impacts must the project support?
cards.answer:
The results should lay the cryptographic foundations for secure future quantum and hybrid networks in Europe.
The expected outcomes are new primitives and protocols beyond QKD, critical analysis of their security and performance against classical counterparts, fundamental insights into quantum information processing and its limits, and a roadmap for quantum cryptography and network functions. The wider destination aims at robust digital infrastructures that resist cyberattacks. No quantified targets are set.

cards.title: Who it suits
cards.question: Who may lead, which partners must take part, and how must the work be shared?
cards.answer:
University and research groups in quantum information science and in applied post-quantum cryptography.
Proposals should include, in a balanced way, quantum scientists and post-quantum cryptography researchers with experience in real-world, applied cryptography. Any beneficiary may coordinate. The consortium needs at least three independent legal entities from three different EU Member States or Horizon Europe associated countries (non-EU countries taking part in the programme), at least one in a Member State. Participation is limited to entities established in those countries and not controlled, directly or indirectly, from a non-eligible country. The call sets no rule on how work or budget are split; the lump-sum budget table fixes each partner's share.

cards.title: Innovation
cards.question: How new must the project be, and in what must it innovate?
cards.answer:
The project must create genuinely new knowledge: new cryptographic paradigms, primitives and protocols.
It is a Research and Innovation Action judged on ambition beyond the state of the art. The innovation lies in technology and theory: quantum and hybrid cryptographic primitives and protocols, their security proofs and a roadmap for their realisation.

cards.title: Maturity
cards.question: Which maturity level is expected at the start and end of the project?
cards.answer:
The call sets no Technology Readiness Level (TRL, a 1–9 scale of maturity).
The work is foundational research; as a Research and Innovation Action it may at most reach validation in a laboratory or simulated environment.

cards.title: Demonstration and integration of work
cards.question: Where must the solution be demonstrated, and how must the work fit with existing systems?
cards.answer:
No demonstration is required; the work is theoretical research, analysis and a roadmap.
The call asks for security proofs, performance analysis and a roadmap that identifies hardware and architecture settings for near-term and long-term quantum networks, but it does not require tests in real operating conditions or integration with existing infrastructure.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Civil Security for Society · pp. 171–173 · HORIZON-CL3-2027-02-CS-ECCC-04, Expected outcome and Scope

call_overview.title: Relevance to TenneT
call_overview.question: Why is this call relevant to TenneT?

cards.title: Why it matters to TenneT
cards.question: Why does this call matter to TenneT, and why can't TenneT take part itself?
cards.answer:
In the long term, quantum-safe protection of grid control and data-exchange links may build on protocols from research like this.
This is our interpretation. The topic does not mention energy; its results are foundational and would reach grid operators only through suppliers of communication and security equipment, years after the project. It links to TenneT's work on operational-technology security in the SylWin1 HVDC retrofit and on grid cybersecurity in TwinEU only through the shared security aim. TenneT cannot realistically take part: although any eligible organisation may join, the work is theoretical research by quantum scientists and cryptographers, with no use case, demonstration or user role that a grid operator could fill.

funding_timing_submission.title: Funding
funding_timing_submission.question: How much funding can the project receive?

cards.title: Funding envelope
cards.answer:
The Commission estimates an EU contribution of EUR 4 million per project, within a topic budget of EUR 4 million for one to two projects.
- Grant request: EUR 4 million per project, shared by all partners; proposals requesting other amounts may still be submitted and selected
- Funding form: lump sum (a fixed amount agreed in advance for the whole project, paid against completed work rather than against costs)
The budgets depend on the EU's 2027 budget; final topic budgets may change by up to 20% after evaluation.

cards.title: Funding rate and co-financing
cards.answer:
All participants can receive up to 100% of their eligible costs; no own contribution is required.
With a lump sum the rate is already applied when the amount is fixed. The call sets no cash or in-kind co-financing condition.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, General Annexes · pp. 31–32 · Form of grant, funding rate and maximum grant amount

funding_timing_submission.title: Timing
funding_timing_submission.question: What timing should the proposal submission and project follow?

cards.title: Application route
cards.answer:
One stage: a full proposal is due by 15 September 2027 through the EU Funding & Tenders Portal.
- Stage 1 — Full proposal: 15 September 2027, 17:00 Brussels time. Part A (an online administrative form, including the budget summary) and Part B (the technical description, at most 45 pages for a lump-sum Research and Innovation Action), submitted by the coordinator
- Opening: 2 March 2027. The ECCC (the European Cybersecurity Competence Centre, the EU body that runs this call for the Commission) may open the call up to one month earlier or later and delay the deadline by up to two months

cards.title: Project window
cards.answer:
The call states no project duration or start date; the grant agreement fixes both.
- Maximum duration: not set by the call; the duration is fixed in months in the grant agreement and extended only exceptionally
- Required start: normally after the grant agreement is signed; an earlier start is possible only exceptionally, for justified reasons and with the granting authority's agreement
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, General Annexes · pp. 30–31 · G — Starting date & project duration

cards.title: Decision and contracting
cards.answer:
Indicatively, results come about 5 months after the deadline and grant agreements are signed about 8 months after it.
- Expected invitation or assessment result: around February 2028 (about 5 months after the deadline; indicative)
- Grant agreement: around May 2028 (about 8 months after the deadline; indicative)
- Conditions before starting: an invitation to grant preparation is not yet a funding commitment, since legal entity validation, financial capacity and exclusion checks follow; if classified information is involved, no grant agreement can be signed until at least one beneficiary holds a facility security clearance

funding_timing_submission.question: Mandatory information to include in the application

cards.title: Evaluation and selection — scored or ranked
cards.answer:
Experts score Excellence, Impact and Quality of implementation out of 5 each; a proposal needs at least 3 on each and 10 overall.
- Evaluation criteria: Excellence (clear objectives, ambition beyond the state of the art, sound methodology); Impact (credible pathway to the topic's expected outcomes, dissemination and exploitation measures); Quality and efficiency of implementation (work plan, risks, resources, and the capacity and role of each partner)
- Thresholds: 3 out of 5 per criterion and 10 out of 15 overall
- Ranking rules: proposals above the thresholds are funded in ranking order within the available budget
- Budget assessment: the lump sum is fixed from the budget table, and the grant may be lower than requested

cards.title: Conditional and exceptional requirements
cards.answer:
Security-sensitive results may restrict dissemination and delay the grant agreement.
- Conditional — classified or sensitive information: some activities may use classified background or produce security-sensitive results; the security rules of the General Annexes then apply, and if classified information is involved no grant agreement can be signed until at least one beneficiary holds a facility security clearance.
